title: Perplexity launches Time Machine for date-stamped web history, up to 365 days back
summary: On Nov. 25, Perplexity added a snapshot_as_of parameter to the Search and Context APIs, so search and full-page reading use only saved copies from on or before the chosen date, up to 365 days back.
ai_summary: Perplexity launched Time Machine for the Search and Context APIs, adding a snapshot_as_of parameter that limits search and full-page reading to saved page copies from on or before a chosen date, up to 365 days back. It prevents hindsight leakage: a model searching today's web can see already-published outcomes, making it impossible to test forecasts fairly. After using it to train GLM-5.3 Flash to forecast 2026 events, the company says held-out scores rose from 0.77 to 0.80, above the market's 0.79. Historical queries cost no extra (Search: $5 per 1,000 requests; Context: $1 per 1,000 URLs). It's aimed at teams doing prediction markets, financial backtests, and reproducible evaluation; the lookback cap is currently 365 days.
brief: Add snapshot_as_of to an existing request and search and reading use only page copies saved on or before that time — no new endpoint required.
You can look back up to 365 days, and history keeps accumulating after that; earlier dates aren't queryable yet.
No price premium: the Search API costs $5 per 1,000 requests, the Context API costs $1 per 1,000 URLs, and existing API keys work as-is.
Perplexity compared it with Exa Snapshot: across 1,000 random queries, only 0.25% of Time Machine pages were flagged as containing hindsight information.

sections.h: What it is: a parameter that sends search and reading back in time

blocks.p: A common way to evaluate an agent — an AI that can search the web, reason, and give an answer — is to ask a question about the past and see whether its judgment at the time matches what actually happened. For example, "Who will win this election?" But to be fair, the agent must see only what was available then, not the results published later.

On Nov. 25, Perplexity launched Time Machine for the Search API and Context API: developers add a snapshot_as_of parameter to a request, and search and full-page reading use only page copies saved at or before that moment — essentially a back-in-time switch for the web.
The key number up front: you can go back up to 365 days from today, and the history keeps growing with every crawl. There's no new endpoint — just a parameter on existing requests.

sections.h: How it works: each URL builds a timestamped history, and queries read copies at or before the cutoff

blocks.p: Each time Perplexity crawls a page, it saves a copy and records when it was saved. Over time, each URL accumulates a version history; Time Machine answers from that history and never touches the live web.

snapshot_as_of is the cutoff for that history. In search, retrieval only considers pages published or first crawled by the cutoff; each candidate is swapped for the latest copy saved at or before the cutoff, and ranking scores the query against that older text. A page that was later updated with the outcome can't rank on future information, and the returned title, date, and snippet all come from that same older copy.

Full-page reading works through the Context API: it returns each URL's full-text copy at the cutoff and never contacts the live site. A typical workflow searches first and then reads pages, so the same cutoff applies to both steps.

sections.h: Why going back matters: today's web hands the answer to the model

blocks.p: Why does this matter? Because the live web already knows how everything turned out. Ask a model today what people knew before an election, and what it finds is often an article that already reports the result. Time Machine lets an agent work at that point in the past, and lets developers score it against what happened later.
That score measures how well the agent researches and forecasts, and whether a new model, prompt, or retrieval setup improves it.

The scoring logic follows the example Perplexity gives: a model estimates an 80% chance that a candidate wins. If the candidate does win, forecasting 80% earns a higher score than forecasting 50%; if the candidate loses, forecasting 80% earns a lower score. That score is the reward signal in reinforcement learning — the feedback that gradually improves the model.

sections.h: Testing it: training a forecasting agent lifts 0.77 to 0.80, above the market's 0.79

blocks.p: Perplexity used reinforcement learning to train GLM-5.3 Flash to forecast real 2026 political events listed on Polymarket, a prediction-market platform. For each question, the task was to estimate the probability of the event as of the day the question was asked.

Before training, the model scored 0.94 on held-out questions while searching the live web — but that's closer to looking up the answer, because the pages it found already reported the outcomes. With search swapped for Time Machine, the same questions scored 0.77; the market itself, using Polymarket prices on the day each question was asked and scored the same way, scored 0.79.

They then trained the model twice: once with the live web and once with Time Machine. With the live web, every question could find the answer directly, so about 90% of training batches had zero gradient and taught the model nothing; with Time Machine, only about 25% did. Finally, held-out questions were retested under Time Machine, and the score rose from 0.77 to 0.80, above the market's 0.79.

sections.h: Versus Exa Snapshot: fewer pages contain hindsight

blocks.p: Perplexity compared Time Machine with Exa Snapshot, another service that provides historical page snapshots, across three sets of 1,000 queries each: random Time Machine queries, news queries, and prediction-market research queries. Both services used the same cutoff for each query.
First, they checked whether returned pages carried publication dates. Time Machine attached dates to 98.8% to 99.5% of returned pages across the three sets, compared with 66.1% to 77.7% for Exa.

A publication date alone isn't enough — an article published before an election could be updated later to declare the winner. So Perplexity had an automated judge read every page and flag any content from after the query's cutoff. Fewer than 0.5% of Time Machine pages were flagged in each set, a lower rate than Exa's in all three. The biggest gap was in the random sample: 0.25% of Time Machine pages were flagged, versus 1.10% of Exa's. Across those 1,000 queries, 18 returned at least one flagged page with Time Machine, versus 62 with Exa.

sections.h: Pricing: same as the standard API, no surcharge

blocks.p: Historical queries carry no surcharge and cost the same as any other Perplexity API call: the Search API is $5 per 1,000 requests, and the Context API is $1 per 1,000 URLs fetched. Existing API keys work right away.
Time Machine requests have a default rate limit; contact the Perplexity API team for higher limits. Pricing for higher tiers isn't stated in the source.

fig.title: Historical queries cost no extra; pricing matches the standard API
fig.subtitle: Amber marks the two APIs opened with this update. Units: US dollars; Search per 1,000 requests, Context per 1,000 URLs.

sections.h: How to use it: same endpoint, one parameter

blocks.p: No new endpoint or extra setup: add snapshot_as_of to an existing Search API or Context API request, and the response reflects the web at that time. Leave it out, and the request returns today's web.
Below is the official Search API example: set the cutoff to 2026-10-20, restrict the search to python.org, and each result's title and snippet come from the copy saved that day.

fig.title: Search API: add snapshot_as_of and search returns that day's web
fig.subtitle: Code reproduced verbatim from the official example
fig.code:
from perplexity import Perplexity

client = Perplexity()

search = client.search.create(
    query="Latest Python 3 Release on the Python Source Releases page",
    snapshot_as_of="2026-10-20T00:00:00Z",
    search_domain_filter=["python.org"],
    max_results=5,
)

for result in search.results:
    print(result.title, result.url)

blocks.p: The Context API works the same way: add a cutoff to a known URL and you can read the full text as it was then. In the official example, the Python Source Releases page on 2026-10-20 still listed Python 3.15 as the latest release, rather than the newer version on today's page.

list: Whether history older than 365 days can be queried: the source only says the lookback reaches "up to 365 days back from today"; earlier dates are currently outside the queryable range.
What the exact rate limit is: the source only says there's a default and that higher limits require contacting the team; per-second or per-minute figures aren't given.
How the 0.94, 0.77, and 0.80 scores are calculated or what units they use: the source only says higher is better and doesn't disclose the scoring formula.

Exa's exact out-of-bound rates for the news and prediction-market query sets: the source gives only 0.25% versus 1.10% for the random sample; for the other two sets it only says Time Machine was lower.
Whether higher rate limits cost extra: the source only says to contact the API team and doesn't list a price.
Whether it's available on all plans and in all regions: the source only says existing API keys can use it and doesn't mention plan differences.

blocks.p: Value: it keeps hindsight answers out of search, so scores reflect a model's actual research and forecasting ability, and evaluations become reproducible.
Cost: you pay per API call; there's a default rate limit; the lookback cap is currently 365 days.

list: If you're training forecasting or research agents, backtesting financial signals, or building reproducible benchmarks: worth trying, especially for separating "lookup" from actual prediction.
If you need to audit historical pages — what a pricing page, terms of service, or changelog said on different dates — the Context API's point-in-time full-text reading covers it.
If you just want to occasionally see an old page and avoid API billing: it works, but estimate your call volume first.
If you need history from more than a year ago: not yet possible; the lookback cap is 365 days.
